topics.title: How Health Policy Is Made and Why It Matters
topics.summary: Health policy is the laws, rules, and decisions that shape what nurses may do, how care is paid for, and how safe care is.
objectives: You can tell public policy from private policy and say who enforces each.
You can explain how a bill becomes law and then regulation.
You can use the rule hierarchy to judge if an action is within legal scope.
You can apply the four essential questions and four policymaking stages.
You can explain evidence-informed policy using the naloxone standing order.
You can choose proper-channel ways to change a policy.
topics.bigPicture:
Health policy is the decisions that government and other groups make to reach health goals. It includes the law that created your license and the hospital rule on restraint checks. It also includes the insurance rule that sets what a client pays for an inhaler. Policy shows up on your unit every shift.

Nurses care because policy decides what you must, may, and must not do. Some rules carry the force of law, and some do not. Once you can sort a rule by who made it, most scope questions get easy. Policy also decides whether your client can reach and afford care.
recap: Health policy includes laws, regulations, guidelines, position statements, resolutions, court decisions, and budget priorities.
Public policy (law and regulation) is legally enforceable. Private policy (hospitals, accreditors, associations) is not law.
Legislatures pass broad laws. Agencies, like the board of nursing, write detailed regulations with the force of law.
Facility policy can be stricter than the law, never looser. Follow the most restrictive rule.
Four questions: target population, cost versus benefit, stakeholders, scientific evidence.
Four stages: agenda setting, government response, implementation, evaluation.
Budget due the first Monday in February; fiscal year starts October 1; continuing resolutions fill gaps.
Evidence-informed policy blends research with values, as in the 2018 NC naloxone standing order.

keyTerms.def: Actions by government and other groups to reach health goals, such as laws, regulations, guidelines, position statements, court decisions, and budgets.
Policy set in law or regulation by government. Government agencies can enforce it.
Policy from hospitals, accreditors, or professional groups. Not law, but it strongly shapes practice.
A broad rule passed by a legislature and signed by the President or governor.
A detailed rule an executive agency writes to carry out a law. It has the force of law but cannot exceed that law.
A government agency that carries out laws, such as the CDC, a health department, or a board of nursing.
The law that empowers an agency and limits the regulations it may write.
The state law that defines nursing, creates the board of nursing, and sets legal scope of practice.
Anyone affected by a policy or able to affect it: clients, nurses, payers, associations, lawmakers.
Policy that blends scientific evidence with stakeholder and lawmaker values and ethics (Box 47.1).
A pre-approved order that lets qualified staff give a set treatment to anyone who meets set criteria.
A temporary law that keeps the federal government funded when Congress misses the October 1 deadline.
A plan’s list of covered drugs. Generics usually cost the client less than brand-name drugs.
Using data to make care safer, such as testing a change with a Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle.

sections.heading: What counts as health policy?
sections.keyIdea: Health policy is any law, rule, or decision that steers health care, so always ask who made it.
sections.body:
Health policy is broader than “the law.” It is any action government or other groups take to reach health goals.

The key sorting rule is public versus private. Public policy is law or regulation written by government. A state can fine a facility or discipline a license for breaking it.

Private policy comes from hospitals, accreditors, and nursing associations. It is not law, but it has real power. Ignoring hospital policy can bring employer discipline.

Private groups also shape public policy by testifying, lobbying, and commenting on proposed rules. That is one reason nurses join associations.
bullets: Laws (statutes) and regulations (rules)
Agency guidelines, such as CDC isolation guidance
Position statements and resolutions from professional groups
Judicial decrees: court decisions that interpret laws
Budget priorities: what gets funded
Vetoes and executive orders, which can carry the force of law

table.caption: Public vs. private health policy
rows: Not law; enforced by jobs, contracts, accreditation
Nurse practice act; board of nursing rules; Medicare law
Restraint policy; Joint Commission standards; ANA Code of Ethics

check.q: A hospital practice council writes a new unit policy. Public or private, and what is its limit?
check.a: Private. It binds employees but cannot allow anything the practice act or board rules forbid.

sections.heading: Law, regulation, policy: which rule wins?
sections.keyIdea: Law sets the outer limit, regulations add detail, and facility policy may be stricter but never looser.
sections.body:
The legislative branch makes laws. Federally, Congress passes a bill and the President signs it, or Congress overrides a veto. In a state, the legislature passes it and the governor signs it.

Laws use broad words so they last. The executive branch carries them out. The enabling statute lets an agency write regulations with the details. Regulations have the force of law but cannot go beyond the law. The courts interpret laws, and their decisions also bind.

When rules conflict, use this order: law, regulation, facility policy, unit procedure. A lower rule may be stricter, never looser. So follow the most restrictive rule that applies.

Delegation works the same way. Law and board rules set the limits, job descriptions narrow them, and the RN decides for each client.
steps: A problem gets attention, such as rising overdose deaths.
Legislators introduce a bill; committees hold hearings where nurses may testify.
Both chambers pass it and the executive signs it. It is now a statute.
An agency drafts regulations, posts them for public comment, and finalizes them.
Organizations write policies that comply. Outcomes are evaluated.

table.caption: Which rule wins?
rows: Policy allows what the practice act does not
Follow the law; do not do it; tell the manager
Stricter still fits inside the law
Order conflicts with law or policy
Clarify with prescriber; use chain of command
The nurse is accountable for scope
Act within scope and standards; propose a policy
A gap is a safety issue

sections.example: A float nurse hears, “Our unit lets aides adjust oxygen.” Policy alone is not enough. The task must be on the aide’s approved list, competency must be documented, and the RN must judge it safe. Titrating oxygen to a goal takes nursing judgment, so the nurse does it and asks for a policy review.

sections.heading: What makes a policy proposal strong?
sections.keyIdea: A strong proposal answers four questions and blends research with the values of the people it affects.
sections.body:
Before anyone drafts a bill, ask four questions (see bullets). Use them for unit changes, too.

Evidence-informed policy blends scientific evidence with the values and concerns of stakeholders and lawmakers.

Box 47.1 shows this with naloxone, which reverses opioid overdose. Research showed high overdose risk after rehab, because tolerance drops. It showed laypeople can use naloxone safely, like epinephrine auto-injectors. Lawmakers still worried about cost, liability, and “enabling.” Evidence alone rarely passes a bill. Advocates must also address these values and concerns.

The result was a 2018 North Carolina State Health Director standing order. Pharmacists could dispense naloxone to anyone who asked, with no individual prescription.
bullets: Target population: Who benefits? Is the group large, underserved, or poor?
Cost versus benefit: Do benefits outweigh the cost?
Stakeholders: Who supports or opposes it, and why?
Scientific evidence: Does research show it works elsewhere?
sections.example: One nurse tells a county board, “This is unfair.” Another says, “It affects 4,000 uninsured children, costs less than the ER visits it prevents, has school nurse support, and worked in two nearby states.” The second answers all four questions.
sections.analogy: Evidence without values is a car with no driver. Values without evidence is a driver with no car.

sections.heading: What are the four stages of policymaking?
sections.keyIdea: Policy moves from agenda setting to government response, implementation, and evaluation; cue words in the stem reveal the stage.
sections.body:
Agenda setting is when a problem gets enough attention that leaders act. Government response is formal action, like passing a bill or proposing a rule.

Implementation puts policy into action with rules, funding, and training. Evaluation asks if it met its goals, at what cost, and with what side effects.

Nurses help at every stage. Funding is policy, too. A program approved but never funded does nothing.
bullets: The President submits a budget by the first Monday in February.
Congress passes appropriations bills before the fiscal year begins October 1.
If not done, a continuing resolution keeps funding at current levels; without one, a shutdown can occur.
Ask for funding while bills are drafted, not after the year starts.

table.caption: Recognize the stage from the cue
rows: Write rules, fund, train, roll out
Train on a new naloxone protocol

check.q: Nurses compare sepsis deaths before and after a screening law. Which stage?
check.a: Evaluation: measuring whether the policy met its goal.

sections.heading: How does policy shape your daily practice?
sections.keyIdea: Policy sets your legal scope, your unit’s procedures, your client’s access to care, and how quality improves.
sections.body:
The course names seven areas shaped by policy (Figure 47.1, bullets).

Access. Coverage drives access, and policy drives billing and payment. Formularies set drug costs. If a client cannot afford a brand-name drug, ask the prescriber about a generic.

Legal scope. The Constitution leaves regulation of professions to the states. Boards of nursing, or “umbrella boards,” enforce practice acts. A current license is required, and a manager’s order is no defense.

Quality. AHRQ (part of DHHS) builds tools and quality indicators that hospitals use to meet Joint Commission goals. Nurses join QI projects, such as a PDSA test of a fall bundle.
bullets: Legal scope of practice
Professional standards (ANA standards, Code of Ethics)
Accreditation standards
Facility policies and procedures
Staffing policies
Public health policies (immunization, disease reporting, smoking bans)
Access to care, plus education, workforce, and research funding

check.q: An RN finds her license expired at midnight. She has five clients. What first?
check.a: Tell the charge nurse so clients are reassigned, and give no care until it is renewed. Even one shift is unlicensed practice.

sections.heading: How can a nurse change a policy?
sections.keyIdea: Change policy with evidence through proper channels; until it changes, follow it unless it would clearly harm the client.
sections.body:
The ANA Code of Ethics calls on nurses to help shape health policy. Inside a hospital, use the proper channel: bring evidence to your manager or practice council, pilot the change, and get approval.

Do not ignore an old policy, vent online, or tell coworkers to “just do it the new way.” Until a policy changes, follow it. If following it would clearly harm the client, protect the client and escalate.
bullets: Contact legislators with data and a client story without identifiers
Testify at hearings
Comment on proposed regulations
Join an association that lobbies
Serve on councils and QI teams
Vote and serve on boards
sections.example: A nurse reads a review showing the unit’s skin care procedure is out of date. She keeps following it for now and brings the review to the practice council.

sections.heading: Common traps: rules that look alike
sections.keyIdea: Most errors come from mixing up who made a rule and how much legal force it carries.
sections.body: These pairs are easy to confuse under time pressure. Use the right-hand column to tell them apart.

table.caption: Law, regulation, and policy look-alikes
rows: Law: legislature, broad. Regulation: agency, detailed.
Regulation has force of law. Policy may be stricter, never broader.
Government wrote it = public. Organization = private.
Agencies carry out laws. Courts interpret them.
A multistate nurse follows the law where the client is.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Policy items look like practice questions; the right answer keeps the nurse inside the law and protects the client.
sections.body:
Health policy items are usually framed as practice choices. Watch for the patterns in the bullets.

Sample question: A charge nurse tells a new RN, “Our hospital policy lets unlicensed assistive personnel do the initial admission assessment when we are short-staffed. Assign it to the aide.” Which response by the new RN is best?

A. “I will assign it because hospital policy authorizes it.”
B. “Initial assessment is an RN responsibility under the nurse practice act. I will complete it and ask that the policy be reviewed.”
C. “I will let the aide do it and then cosign the assessment.”
D. “I will ask the client whether they mind the aide doing it.”
bullets: Policy conflicts with legal scope: follow the law and escalate.
Which agency or branch? Boards and health departments are executive.
Best advocacy? Evidence plus proper channels.
Name the stage from cue words.
steps: Read the stem: hospital policy conflicts with RN scope.
What is it asking? Which rule controls: hospital policy or the practice act?
Key cues: initial assessment is an RN duty; “unlicensed” means no license to assess; “short-staffed” is pressure, not authority.
A is wrong: policy cannot expand legal scope. C is wrong: cosigning may falsify the record. D is wrong: client permission cannot authorize it.
The answer is B: it follows the law, protects the client, and fixes the policy properly.
Strategy: name each rule’s source, rank by legal force, and act inside the strictest rule.

sections.heading: Worked case: a school naloxone policy
sections.keyIdea: Fix a gap with a formal policy through proper channels, not an informal workaround.
sections.body:
Ms. Alvarez, RN, is a school nurse in a rural county. Two students’ parents died of opioid overdoses this year. Naloxone is available at pharmacies under a state standing order, but the district has no policy on staff keeping or giving it.

The principal says, “Just keep some in your bag and use it if something happens.” Ms. Alvarez wants to help students and staff while staying within the law and district policy.
steps: Cues: overdose deaths, no district policy, and an informal shortcut.
Rules: state law and the standing order govern access; district policy governs staff. The principal’s comment is not policy.
Four questions: students and staff; kit cost vs. deaths prevented; parents, board, health department; safety data.
Stage: agenda setting, bringing data to the school board.
Act: draft a proposal with the health department and offer to lead training.
Evaluate: track training, kit supply, and doses given.

check.q: The board adopts the policy, and Ms. Alvarez starts training staff to spot overdose and give naloxone. Which stage is this, and what comes next?
check.a: Implementation. Next is evaluation: measure training reach, kit supply, response times, and outcomes, then revise the policy if needed.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, the legislature wrote the Nursing Practice Act, and the Board of Nursing writes the detailed rules.
sections.body: North Carolina shows the law-versus-regulation link clearly. The legislature defined nursing broadly, and the Board filled in the detail.
bullets: The NCBON, an executive agency, regulates nursing under the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). The Act is the statute; Board rules are regulations.
RN and LPN components of practice: 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN).
The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. The LPN works under RN or provider supervision.
The RN may delegate tasks, not the nursing process or judgment. NCBON has a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP and a scope decision tree.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. A nurse with a multistate license must follow the practice laws of the state where the client is.
Box 47.1’s naloxone standing order (2018) is an NC policy.
Good Samaritan law (G.S. 90-21.14): protects unpaid emergency care unless gross negligence, wanton conduct, or intentional wrongdoing. It does not cover paid employment.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Source: Module 47 study guide, pp. 2795–2798 (key terms; Outcomes 47.1–47.3; Figure 47.1; Box 47.1; budget process).
Added: the law–regulation–policy hierarchy and advocacy methods, often tested on the NCLEX.
Update: Joint Commission hospital safety goals became National Performance Goals effective January 1, 2026. Names and numbers may differ from older sources.
Added: PDSA as a standard QI model.

mnemonics.name: LEG makes, EXEC takes
mnemonics.text: The LEGislature makes the law. The EXECutive agency takes it and writes the detailed regulations. The board of nursing is EXEC.

mnemonics.name: A-G-I-E: “A Good Idea Evolves”
mnemonics.text: Agenda setting → Government response → Implementation → Evaluation: the four stages of policymaking.

mnemonics.name: “People, Price, Players, Proof”
mnemonics.text: The four questions: target Population, cost vs. benefit (Price), stakeholders (Players), and scientific evidence (Proof).

pearls: A regulation carries the force of law but can never go beyond the law that authorizes it.
Facility policy can be stricter than the law, never looser. Follow the most restrictive rule.
Boards of nursing are executive branch agencies. They license, discipline, and write rules that add detail to the practice act.
Licensure is personal. A manager’s order or facility policy will not protect a nurse who works outside legal scope.
Strong advocacy combines evidence, cost data, stakeholder analysis, and a client story without identifiers.
redFlags: A policy or supervisor tells you to do or delegate a task your state law does not allow. Do not do it; protect the client and escalate.
A client cannot afford a medication and plans to skip doses. Work with the prescriber on generic or formulary options and refer for financial help.
Your license has lapsed. Practicing without a current license breaks the practice act, even if your employer knows.

checks.q: A hospital policy lets LPNs write the initial plan of care for new admissions. A new RN asks if that makes it legal. How should the preceptor answer?
checks.a: No. Facility policy cannot expand legal scope. Initial comprehensive assessment and planning are RN duties under the practice act and board rules. The policy should be reported for review.

checks.q: A nursing association gathers overdose data and client stories to show legislators who have not yet looked at the issue. Which stage is this?
checks.a: Agenda setting. The goal is to get the problem onto lawmakers’ agenda; no formal government action has happened yet.

checks.q: The board of nursing adopts a new rule requiring continuing competence hours for renewal. Is this a law or a regulation, and what limits it?
checks.a: A regulation written by an executive agency. It must be authorized by, and stay within, the nurse practice act.

checks.q: A nurse with a multistate compact license gives telehealth follow-up to a client in another compact state. Whose practice laws apply?
checks.a: The practice laws of the state where the client is located at the time of care.

checks.q: A nurse wants the hospital to adopt an evidence-based fall bundle. What should her proposal include, and where should it go?
checks.a: The target population, cost versus benefit, stakeholder support and concerns, and supporting research or models. She brings it to the practice council or the right committee.

topics.title: Health Agencies, Accreditation, and Nursing Associations
topics.summary: Agencies carry out health policy, accreditors like The Joint Commission judge quality, and associations set standards and lobby.
objectives: You can match a health problem to the right federal, state, local, or international agency.
You can name what DHHS divisions, OSHA, and EPA do, with a bedside example.
You can tell licensure and board approval from voluntary accreditation.
You can explain Joint Commission safety goals, sentinel events, and your role in a survey.
You can choose the best professional association for a nurse’s need.
topics.bigPicture:
Laws do nothing until an agency carries them out. The CDC tracks outbreaks, CMS pays for Medicare, and OSHA makes sure you have sharps containers. Your state licenses hospitals, and your county inspects restaurants. Knowing who does what lets you send clients to the right place.

Accreditation is a voluntary seal of quality from a private group, such as The Joint Commission. On survey day, surveyors talk to bedside nurses, so you must explain your unit’s practice and its evidence. Professional associations give nurses one strong voice. They set standards, support learning, and lobby.
recap: DHHS is the main federal health agency. Match each division to its job: CDC disease, CMS payment, FDA drugs, AHRQ quality.
OSHA (Department of Labor) protects workers. EPA protects the environment. Neither is part of DHHS.
States license facilities, handle complaints, and track vital statistics. Counties do sanitation and prevention. Cities run clinics.
WHO is multilateral, USAID is bilateral, and Project Hope and World Central Kitchen are NGOs.
Licensure and board program approval are required. Certification and accreditation are voluntary.
The Joint Commission sets yearly safety goals, expects root cause analysis of sentinel events, and questions bedside staff.
Associations set standards and ethics, support research and education, and lobby. Match the group to the need.

keyTerms.def: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the main federal health agency. It works through divisions such as CDC, CMS, FDA, and NIH.
Occupational Safety and Health Administration, part of the Department of Labor. It requires employers to remove workplace hazards.
Environmental Protection Agency. It protects air, water, and land, which affects population health.
State executive agency that controls disease, licenses facilities, handles complaints, and tracks vital statistics.
Official records of births, deaths, marriages, and divorces, kept by the state.
Nutrition program for pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women, infants, and children under 5 at nutritional risk.
International group funded by many governments, often through the United Nations, such as WHO.
One country’s government agency that gives aid to developing nations, such as USAID.
Nongovernmental or private voluntary organization, independent of any government, such as Project Hope.
Required government permission to practice (nurse) or to operate (facility).
Voluntary proof of an individual nurse’s specialty knowledge, usually by exam.
Voluntary, private peer review showing an organization meets quality standards. It needs periodic review and site visits.
A safety event causing death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm. It requires a root cause analysis.
A structured review of a serious event that looks for system and process failures, not someone to blame.
A survey method where surveyors follow one client’s care and ask staff what they do and why.
A membership group that sets standards and ethics, supports research and education, and lobbies.

sections.heading: Which federal agency handles what?
sections.keyIdea: Ask if the problem is client care, worker safety, or the environment: that points to DHHS, OSHA, or EPA.
sections.body:
The Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) is the main federal health agency. It gives out more grant money than all other federal agencies combined. The course cites a FY 2021 budget of $94.5 billion discretionary and $1.3 trillion mandatory. You need the divisions, not the numbers (see table).

Two agencies outside DHHS matter. OSHA is part of the Department of Labor. It protects workers, for example by requiring sharps containers, safety needles, and eyewash stations.

The EPA protects air, water, and land. That shapes problems such as asthma and lead exposure.

table.caption: DHHS operating divisions
rows: Older adults and people with disabilities in the community
Services that delay nursing home placement
AHRQ (Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality)
Research and tools for safety and quality
Quality indicators used in hospital QI
ATSDR (Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry)
CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
Runs Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP; payment rules
No payment for some hospital-acquired conditions
Drug recalls; MedWatch adverse event reports
Care for American Indian and Alaska Native peoples
SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration)
Mental health and substance use services

sections.example: A nurse gets a needlestick from a syringe with no safety feature. First, she washes the site with soap and water. Then she reports to her supervisor and employee health for follow-up and files an incident report. OSHA requires safer devices, so she also reports the unsafe syringe.

check.q: A client asks where to report a serious reaction to a new drug. Which agency program applies?
check.a: The FDA’s MedWatch program. The nurse also follows facility reporting steps.

sections.heading: What do state and local agencies do?
sections.keyIdea: States license and inspect facilities, counties protect the community, cities run clinics, and social services enroll people in programs.
sections.body:
State health agencies are part of the state executive branch. They report to the governor and follow federal guidelines. A state Office of EMS (OEMS) sets EMS training standards, oversees trauma systems, and licenses ambulances.

Local social services offices usually run Medicaid, CHIP, and WIC. For referrals, think “the nearest level that delivers the service.”
bullets: State: control infectious disease and do outbreak contact tracing
State: address health inequities; enforce county rules and statewide laws, like smoking bans
State: license facilities (hospitals, long-term care, child care, labs) and resolve complaints
State: track vital statistics
County: sanitation, food safety, waste disposal, child care sanitation
County: injury prevention, like smoke detectors, bike helmets, car seats, and lead screening
City: free clinics, HIV and sexual health testing, TB clinics, dental clinics

table.caption: Match the need to the level
rows: Unsafe care in a licensed nursing home
Free TB testing for a shelter resident

sections.example: Clinical Example A: Richard Taylor works at a homeless shelter and tests positive for TB. The city health department had not screened there. The nurse refers him to a free or low-cost TB clinic. She also asks the city and state health departments for routine shelter TB screening. That is care for one client and for the population.

check.q: Parents ask where to get a free infant car seat and learn to install it. Which level helps?
check.a: The county health department, which runs injury-prevention programs.

sections.heading: How are international groups sorted?
sections.keyIdea: Ask who funds and controls it: many governments (multilateral), one government (bilateral), or none (NGO).
sections.body:
Multilateral groups are funded by many governments, often through the UN. The World Health Organization (WHO) is the top one and the only one with legal authority. Members agreed to binding rules, like the International Health Regulations.

Bilateral agencies belong to one government and aid developing nations. USAID is the classic example.

NGOs, also called PVOs, are independent of government. The U.S. has more than 1.5 million. Project Hope gives medicines, training, and disaster relief. World Central Kitchen gives emergency food.

check.q: A nurse joins a privately funded relief charity after an earthquake abroad. What type of group is it?
check.a: An NGO (PVO), because no government controls it. Do not let size or fame decide; WHO is famous but governmental.

sections.heading: Licensure vs. accreditation: what is the difference?
sections.keyIdea: Licensure and board approval are required by law; certification and accreditation are voluntary marks of quality.
sections.body:
Licensure is required government permission. Nurses get it from the board of nursing, and hospitals from the state health agency. Board approval of a nursing program is also required; it lets graduates take the NCLEX.

Certification is voluntary proof of one nurse’s specialty skill. Accreditation is voluntary peer review of an organization, with regular site visits.

Why do something voluntary? It brings trust, payer credibility, and Medicare and Medicaid payment. Hospitals accredited by a CMS-approved body like TJC are “deemed” to meet Medicare rules. For schools, accreditation matters for RN-to-BSN and graduate admission.
bullets: CCNE (Commission on Collegiate Nursing Education): arm of AACN; baccalaureate and graduate programs, plus some residencies.
ACEN (Accreditation Commission for Education in Nursing): all types, practical nursing through clinical doctorate.
NLN CNEA (NLN Commission for Nursing Education Accreditation): founded 2013, standards 2016; practical through clinical doctorate.
An associate or practical program seeks ACEN or NLN CNEA, not CCNE.
sections.analogy: A driver’s license lets you drive legally. A five-star safety rating is an outside review you invited. You can drive without it, but buyers trust the rated car more.

check.q: A graduate asks, “My program isn’t CCNE- or ACEN-accredited. Can I take the NCLEX?”
check.a: Yes, if the board of nursing approved it. Accreditation may matter later for BSN or graduate school.

sections.heading: What does The Joint Commission expect?
sections.keyIdea: TJC sets yearly safety goals, requires analysis of sentinel events, and expects bedside nurses to explain their practice.
sections.body:
The Joint Commission (TJC) is an independent nonprofit that accredits hospitals and other care settings. In 2003 it began yearly National Patient Safety Goals. For hospitals, these became National Performance Goals in 2026.

A sentinel event causes death, permanent harm, or severe temporary harm, like wrong-site surgery or a fall with a fracture. The organization must do a root cause analysis focused on systems, not blame.

Your role: help write evidence-based policies, join mock surveys and audits, and talk with surveyors. In a tracer, surveyors follow one client and ask staff what they do and why.
bullets: Identify clients with two identifiers
Communicate critical results
Use medications and alarms safely
Prevent infection, including CAUTI
Identify suicide risk
Prevent surgical mistakes (Universal Protocol)
sections.example: Clinical Example B: Darren Langdon, RN, updates his unit’s outdated CAUTI policy using current research. Key points include insertion criteria, sterile insertion, a closed system, the bag below the bladder, and daily review of need. When the surveyor asks, he explains the rates, evidence, new policy, staff teaching, and results.

check.q: During a tracer, a nurse realizes she started an IV antibiotic without checking two identifiers. What first?
check.a: Stop the infusion and verify identity. Then assess the client and report. The surveyor does not change the priority.

steps: Know the safety goals for your unit.
Know where policies are and find them fast.
Explain how a policy was built: problem, evidence, change, results.
If you don’t know, say how you would find out.

sections.heading: Which professional association fits the need?
sections.keyIdea: Match the association to the need: ANA for ethics, NSNA for students, specialty groups for specialty support.
sections.body:
Associations set standards and ethics, support research, and lobby. Many have state branches.

Specialty groups include the Academy of Medical-Surgical Nurses, AANA (nurse anesthesiology), ACNM (nurse-midwives), AANP (nurse practitioners), and NACNS (clinical nurse specialists). Read names carefully: AACN can mean Colleges of Nursing or Critical-Care Nurses.

Demographic groups include the Asian American/Pacific Islander Nurses Association, the American Assembly for Men in Nursing, the National Black Nurses Association, and the National Association of Hispanic Nurses.
bullets: ICN (International Council of Nurses): 130+ national associations; the oldest health professional group. Focus: practice, regulation, and socioeconomic welfare.
STTI (Sigma Theta Tau International): the honor society, founded 1922 at Indiana University; 135,000+ members in 100+ countries; develops leaders.
ANA (American Nurses Association): speaks for 4 million+ RNs; publishes the Code of Ethics and standards of practice.
NSNA (National Student Nurses Association): leadership, scholarships, and career help for students.
AACN (American Association of Colleges of Nursing): voice for BSN and graduate education; 840+ schools.
NLN (National League for Nursing): first U.S. nursing group; diverse workforce and care for the underserved.
sections.example: Clinical Example C: Marsha Johnson, CRNA, is the only nurse anesthetist at a small surgery center and feels isolated. Her best step is joining AANA for peers and continuing education. The ANA is valuable, but the specialty group fits her need best.

check.q: The only nurse-midwife at a rural birth center wants specialty peers and education. Which group fits?
check.a: The American College of Nurse-Midwives (ACNM), her specialty association.

sections.heading: Common traps: names that sound alike
sections.keyIdea: Read full names and ask what the organization’s mission is before choosing.
sections.body: Many errors come from similar names and from the word “voluntary.”

table.caption: Agency and accreditation look-alikes
rows: Licensure: required, government. Accreditation: voluntary, private.
Board approval decides NCLEX eligibility. Accreditation does not.
CCNE: BSN and graduate only. ACEN: all levels, including PN and ADN.
Colleges of Nursing = education. Critical-Care Nurses = specialty.
OSHA protects workers. CDC controls disease in the public.
CMS sets payment rules. The state licenses and investigates.
County: community and prevention. City: clinics.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Restate the problem in one word, such as worker, disease, payment, or facility, then match it to the right group.
sections.body:
Expect items on where to refer, how to answer a surveyor, required versus voluntary, and which association fits.

Sample question: A surveyor asks a staff nurse how the unit prevents CAUTI. Which response is best?

A. “Ask my manager; she handles accreditation.”
B. “We use a nurse-driven removal protocol based on evidence, review catheter need daily, and track CAUTI rates monthly.”
C. “Our rate is zero, so we haven’t changed anything.”
D. “I can show you the policy, but I’m not sure why we do it.”
steps: Read the stem: a surveyor questions a staff nurse at the bedside.
What is it asking? The best response showing the nurse’s accreditation role.
Key cue: surveyors expect frontline staff to explain practice and evidence.
A deflects. C shows no ongoing QI. D shows the evidence has not reached practice.
The answer is B: it names the practice, the daily check, and outcome tracking.
Strategy: the best answer explains what we do, why, and how we measure it.

sections.heading: Worked case: TB at a shelter
sections.keyIdea: Protect people first, then refer the client, then fix the system that let the problem happen.
sections.body: Mr. Diaz, 52, stays at a shelter. He has a 4-week cough, night sweats, and weight loss. Three other residents “have the same cough.” He has no insurance, and the shelter does no TB screening. He sits in a crowded waiting room.
steps: Cues: long cough, night sweats, weight loss, group living, and similar cases suggest active TB and a cluster.
Safety first: give him a surgical mask and move him to a separate room. Staff wear N95 respirators.
Notify the provider. TB is reportable, so follow procedure to notify public health.
Refer him to the public health TB clinic for free or low-cost care.
Confirm staff exposure follow-up, a worker-safety issue.
Advocate with the health department for routine shelter screening.

check.q: Which action fixes the population problem, not just his care?
check.a: Asking the city and state health departments for routine TB screening and prevention protocols in shelters.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, the Board of Nursing licenses nurses, two agencies keep aide registries, and county DSS takes maltreatment reports.
bullets: The NCBON licenses RNs and LPNs under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.). Its approval makes program graduates NCLEX-eligible.
Nurse Aide I registry: kept by NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. Nurse Aide II registry: kept by NCBON; NA IIs must also be on the NA I registry.
Tasks must be on the aide’s approved list and the RN must judge delegation right for that client.
NCBON uses a Just Culture Complaint Evaluation Tool: human error vs. at-risk vs. reckless behavior.

Conduct issues (diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, confidentiality breaches) go to the Board, not just the employer. NCBON has alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.

G.S. 7B-301: NC is a universal reporting state. Anyone who suspects a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent must report to county DSS. Report suspicion; do not wait for proof. Good-faith reporters are immune; knowingly failing to report is a crime.
G.S. 108A-102: anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to county DSS.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Source: Module 47 study guide, pp. 2798–2802 (Outcomes 47.4–47.6; Clinical Examples A, B, C; Table 47.1; key term Accreditation, p. 2800).
Sentinel events: TJC requires a response (root cause analysis and action plan). Self-reporting to TJC is encouraged but voluntary.
Safety goals: hospital NPSGs became National Performance Goals on January 1, 2026. CAUTI prevention is still required.
Deemed status: Medicare participation can also come via state survey.
WIC also serves postpartum and breastfeeding women and is often run by local health departments.
OSHA covers most private employers; many public workers fall under state plans.
AANA is now the American Association of Nurse Anesthesiology. DHHS gets reorganized; learn functions.

mnemonics.name: Worker → OSHA; Germs → CDC; Money → CMS; Meds → FDA
mnemonics.text: Sort agency questions by the core problem.

mnemonics.name: County = Community; City = Clinic
mnemonics.text: Counties do sanitation and prevention; cities run TB, HIV, and dental clinics.

pearls: OSHA is in the Department of Labor, not DHHS. It protects workers, not clients.
Board approval, not accreditation, makes a graduate eligible for the NCLEX.
CCNE accredits only BSN and graduate programs.
Surveyors want to hear what you do, why, and how you measure it.
Root cause analysis looks at systems. Report events and near misses promptly.
redFlags: Possible active TB in a group setting: mask the client, isolate, use N95s, and notify the provider. TB is reportable, so follow reporting rules.
A coworker hides an adverse event before a survey: events must be reported and analyzed.
Suspected child abuse during a visit: report the suspicion to the designated agency (county DSS in NC) without waiting for proof.

checks.q: A nursing home leaves residents unattended for hours. Where should a formal complaint go?
checks.a: The state health agency, which licenses facilities and resolves complaints.

checks.q: A practical nursing program director wants CCNE accreditation. What should the educator point out?
checks.a: CCNE accredits only BSN and graduate programs. A PN program would seek ACEN or NLN CNEA.

checks.q: A surveyor asks a nurse the unit’s hand-hygiene rate, and she doesn’t know it. Best response?
checks.a: Answer honestly, describe the practice and its monitoring, and say where the data are kept.

checks.q: A fall causes a hip fracture. What process follows, and what is its focus?
checks.a: A root cause analysis of a sentinel event, focused on system failures, followed by an action plan.

checks.q: At a WIC visit, a 3-year-old has bruises in different stages on the back and arms. What first?
checks.a: Report the suspicion to child protective services at county DSS. Do not investigate or wait for proof.

topics.title: Paying for Care: Insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, and the ACA
topics.summary: How care is paid for decides what clients can reach and afford. Nurses spot cost barriers, teach clients to use coverage, and refer early.
objectives: You can define premium, deductible, co-payment, coinsurance, and out-of-pocket maximum.
You can rank private plans from most to least restrictive.
You can tell Medicare Parts A–D, Medigap, Medicaid, and CHIP apart.
You can explain key ACA protections to a client.
You can choose nursing actions that lower cost barriers to care.
topics.bigPicture:
A care plan a client cannot afford will not happen. Clients ration insulin, skip specialists, or avoid the ER because of cost fears. Each is a financing problem with a safety risk, and nurses often hear about it first.

Two ideas carry this topic. Private plans sit on a spectrum: more limits usually mean lower costs, and more freedom costs more. Public programs differ by who qualifies and who pays. Medicare is mostly for people 65+, Medicaid is for low income, and CHIP covers children just above Medicaid limits.
recap: Premium keeps the plan; deductible comes first; co-pay is a set dollar amount; coinsurance is a percent; the maximum caps the year.
Most to least restrictive: HMO, POS, PPO, CDHP, indemnity.
Emergencies are covered under every plan. Never delay emergency care for a referral.
Medicare: 65+, certain disabilities, ESRD, ALS. A = hospital, B = medical, C = Advantage, D = drugs.
Medicare does not pay long-term custodial care. Medicaid is the main public payer for those who qualify.
Medicaid is joint federal-state for low income. CHIP covers children under 19 above Medicaid limits.
ACA: no annual or lifetime limits on essential benefits, dependents to 26, free preventive care, no preexisting-condition denials.

keyTerms.def: What you pay, usually monthly, to keep a plan active, whether or not you use care.
What you pay each year before the plan starts paying its share.
A set dollar amount paid at a visit, such as $20. Specialist co-pays are usually higher.
Your percentage share of a bill after the deductible, such as 20%.
The most you pay for covered care in 12 months. After that, the plan pays 100% of covered fees.
Health maintenance organization: network-only plan with a PCP gatekeeper who gives referrals. Most restrictive.
Primary care provider. In an HMO, the gatekeeper who manages care and refers to specialists.
Point-of-service hybrid: at each visit, choose HMO-style in-network care or costlier out-of-network care.
Preferred-provider organization: no PCP needed, larger network, lower costs in network.
Consumer-driven plan: high deductible, lower premium, paired with an HSA or HRA.
Fee-for-service plan with no network. Least restrictive; may still need preauthorization.
An unmarried partner, of any sex, an employer may cover alongside the employee.
Private supplement that pays Original Medicare’s gaps: co-pays, coinsurance, deductibles.
Help with daily tasks like bathing and dressing. Medicare does not pay for it long term.
Children’s Health Insurance Program: covers children under 19 whose families earn too much for Medicaid.
Supplemental Security Income: cash aid for food, clothing, and housing for aged, blind, or disabled people with little income. Not insurance.

sections.heading: What do insurance cost words mean?
sections.keyIdea: Premium keeps the plan, the deductible comes first, then co-pays or coinsurance, until the yearly maximum is reached.
sections.body:
Every plan uses five cost words (see bullets). Lower premiums usually mean higher deductibles. The out-of-pocket maximum protects against huge bills.

You will not calculate bills at the bedside. But these words help you see why a client is worried and when to refer to financial counseling.
bullets: Premium: paid every month to keep coverage, used or not
Deductible: paid first each year before the plan shares costs
Co-payment: a set dollar amount, like $20 for primary care or $50 for a specialist
Coinsurance: a percent of the bill after the deductible, like 20%
Out-of-pocket maximum: the yearly cap; then the plan pays 100% of covered fees
sections.example: A plan has a $1,500 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and a $5,000 maximum. The client has a $10,000 covered surgery. She pays $1,500, then 20% of the remaining $8,500 ($1,700), for $3,200 total. If she needs a $20,000 stay later that year, she stops paying at $5,000 total.

check.q: A client says, “I pay $400 a month. Why did I get an MRI bill?”
check.a: The premium only keeps the plan active. She likely has not met her deductible and may owe coinsurance.

sections.heading: How restrictive is each private plan?
sections.keyIdea: From most to least restrictive: HMO, POS, PPO, CDHP, indemnity; more freedom usually costs the client more.
sections.body:
“Restrictive” means how much the plan controls which providers you use and whether you need permission first.

An HMO covers only network providers, except emergencies. Members must live or work in its area. A PCP acts as gatekeeper, so specialists need a referral. HMOs stress prevention and cost the least.

A POS plan lets members choose at each visit: in network, or out of network for more money. A PPO needs no PCP and has a bigger network, but co-pays are higher than an HMO’s.

A CDHP is defined by cost design, not network; many use a PPO-style network. An indemnity plan has no network but may require preauthorization for an MRI.

Emergencies are always covered. The ACA requires emergency coverage with no prior approval and in-network cost-sharing.
bullets: CDHP: lower premium, high deductible, paired account
HSA: owned by the employee and portable; employee or employer may add money
HRA: funded and owned by the employer; usually not portable
Risk: clients may skip care before meeting the deductible
ACA preventive care is free in network, even before the deductible

table.caption: Private plans, most to least restrictive

sections.analogy: An HMO is a set menu with a host who seats you. POS lets you order off-menu for extra. A PPO is a big buffet with a discount at house stations. Indemnity is a gift card good anywhere.

check.q: A client with a high-deductible plan stopped his blood pressure pill until he meets his deductible. What first?
check.a: Assess his blood pressure and symptoms. Then ask the prescriber about a cheaper generic, note that HSA money can pay for drugs, and refer for financial help.

sections.heading: How do people get private coverage?
sections.keyIdea: Most adults get coverage through work, so job loss and life changes can cut off medicines and follow-up care.
sections.body:
Employment-sponsored insurance (ESI) covers employees, spouses, dependents, and often domestic partners. It has an out-of-pocket maximum.

Self-employed people may buy individual plans. These were often costlier with less coverage. Before the ACA, insurers could deny people with preexisting conditions.

When job coverage ends, COBRA usually lets a worker keep the same plan for up to 18 months. The client pays the full premium plus a small fee. Job loss also opens a special enrollment period, generally 60 days, for a Marketplace plan. Lower income may also mean Medicaid.
steps: Ask what coverage the client has and whether it will change soon (job, age 26 or 65, divorce, move).
Ask if the client can afford new drugs and visits.
If coverage is ending or unaffordable, refer to case management or social work today.
Document the referral and the plan.

check.q: A client going home after pneumonia was laid off; his coverage ends this month. He needs an inhaler. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Treat the lapse as a safety risk. Refer him today to review COBRA, a Marketplace special enrollment, or Medicaid, and confirm he can get the inhaler.

sections.heading: What does Medicare cover, and what not?
sections.keyIdea: Medicare covers people 65+, certain disabled people, and those with ESRD or ALS, but not long-term custodial care.
sections.body:
Medicare is federal insurance run by CMS. The course says it covers 17.9% of Americans. Ten years of Medicare taxes, by the client or spouse, earns premium-free Part A.

Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care, routine dental or eye care, hearing aids, or cosmetic surgery. Part A covers only short-term skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying hospital stay.

Medigap fills Original Medicare’s gaps. Medicare pays first, then Medigap. Plans have standard letters.
bullets: Age 65 or older
Younger people after 24 months of Social Security disability benefits
ALS: coverage starts with disability benefits, no 24-month wait
End-stage renal disease (ESRD): usually after a short wait once dialysis starts

table.caption: Box 47.2: the four parts of Medicare
rows: Inpatient, short-term skilled SNF, hospice, home health
Premium-free with 10 years of taxes; deductibles, coinsurance
Provider visits, outpatient, home health, DME (walkers, wheelchairs), screenings (mammograms, colonoscopies, flu shots)
Private plan bundling A and B (usually D), often extras
Part B premium plus plan premium

sections.analogy: A for Admitted, B for Bills from providers, C for Combination, D for Drugs.

check.q: A daughter says, “Medicare will pay for Dad to live in the nursing home now that he can’t bathe himself.” How should the nurse respond?
check.a: Explain that Medicare covers only short-term skilled care, not long-term custodial care. Refer to social work to discuss Medicaid, long-term care insurance, or private pay.

sections.heading: Who do Medicaid, CHIP, and other programs cover?
sections.keyIdea: Medicaid is joint federal-state coverage for low income; CHIP covers children under 19 just above Medicaid limits.
sections.body:
Medicaid began in 1965 under Title XIX of the Social Security Act. Federal and state governments fund and run it together. States set rules within federal mandates, so coverage varies. It covers hospital and outpatient care, labs, prenatal care, and nursing home and home care. The ACA expanded it starting in 2014.

Medicaid, not Medicare, is the major public payer for long-term nursing home care. People with both are “dual eligible.”

CHIP (formerly SCHIP) uses federal and matching state funds. It covers checkups, shots, dental, vision, hospital, lab, and x-ray care. States also fund priorities like maternal-child health, smoking cessation, obesity, HIV/AIDS, substance abuse, and environmental health. Public hospitals, like NYC Health + Hospitals and Cook County, give indigent care.

table.caption: Public programs at a glance
rows: Aged, blind, disabled with little income (cash)
American Indian and Alaska Native peoples

check.q: A 46-year-old on dialysis lost his job and plans to skip treatments “until I turn 65.” What first?
check.a: Explain that ESRD may qualify him for Medicare now, and refer him to social work today. Skipping dialysis is dangerous.

sections.heading: What did the Affordable Care Act change?
sections.keyIdea: The ACA widened coverage and added protections clients can use: age 26, free prevention, and no preexisting-condition denials.
sections.body:
The Affordable Care Act (ACA) passed in 2010. It is the biggest financing law since Medicare and Medicaid. It covered more than 20 million uninsured people.

At the bedside, three facts help most: the age-26 rule, preexisting-condition protection, and free preventive care.
bullets: Medicaid expansion (2014) and the Health Insurance Marketplace
No annual or lifetime dollar limits on essential benefits
Dependents may stay on a parent’s plan until 26
Evidence-based preventive services with no cost-sharing
No denial or higher price for preexisting conditions
Limits on unreasonable premium hikes; clear consumer information

check.q: A 25-year-old with asthma says she was dropped from her mom’s plan at 23. What is accurate?
check.a: Dependents can generally stay on a parent’s plan until 26. Asthma cannot be used to deny coverage.

sections.heading: Common traps: money words that sound alike
sections.keyIdea: Medicare is age and disability; Medicaid is income; a co-pay is dollars and coinsurance is percent.
sections.body: Financing terms sound alike. Use this table under time pressure.

table.caption: Financing look-alikes
rows: MediCARE: care for the aged and disabled. MediCAID: aid for low income.
CHIP: children whose family “earns too much for Medicaid.”
Part C replaces Original Medicare. Medigap fills its gaps. Not used together.
HMO needs a PCP referral. PPO does not.
HSA goes with you to a new job. HRA stays with the employer.
SSI is cash. Medicaid is health coverage.
Medicare pays short-term skilled care, not long-term help with bathing.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Physical safety first, then the right coverage rule, then accurate teaching and the right referral.
sections.body:
Items ask you to correct a misconception, match a plan, or remove a cost barrier. Wrong answers often delay care or give false comfort.

Sample question: An HMO member visiting family out of state calls with crushing chest pain for 20 minutes. He asks if he needs a referral first. Which response is best?

A. “Call your PCP first so the visit is covered.”
B. “Call 911 now; emergency care is covered even outside your network.”
C. “Drive to the nearest in-network hospital.”
D. “Find an in-network urgent care online.”
steps: Read the stem: an HMO member has chest pain and asks about referrals.
What is it asking? The best response during a physical emergency.
Key cues: crushing chest pain suggests a heart attack. The HMO detail is a distractor.
A delays care. C is unsafe driving and delay. D is the wrong level of care.
The answer is B: call 911; emergencies are covered without a referral.
Strategy: safety first, coverage questions later.

sections.heading: Worked case: Mrs. Greene goes home
sections.keyIdea: Find the safety risk hidden in the money problem, then fix coverage gaps before discharge.
sections.body: Mrs. Greene, 78, is going home after hip fracture repair. She has Original Medicare (A and B), no Part D, and a small income. She needs a walker, skilled rehab, and a new anticoagulant. She sometimes skips medicines because of cost. Her daughter says Medicare will cover a nursing home forever.
steps: Cues: low income, no drug plan, a new high-risk drug, skipped doses, and a myth about long-term care.
Analyze: Part A covers short-term skilled rehab; Part B covers the walker with 20% coinsurance. No Part D means the drug may be unaffordable.
Priority: skipped anticoagulant doses could cause a clot.
Act: ask the prescriber about a lower-cost option. Refer to social work for Part D, low-income help, and Medicaid.
Teach the daughter kindly that Medicare does not pay permanent custodial care.
Evaluate: before discharge, confirm she can get, afford, and explain each drug.

check.q: Mrs. Greene asks if Medigap would pay for her prescriptions. What is accurate?
check.a: Medigap covers deductibles and coinsurance. Drug coverage comes from Part D or a Medicare Advantage plan with drugs.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, county DSS handles Medicaid and CHIP enrollment and also takes protective-services reports.
bullets: The local social services office in NC is the county department of social services (DSS). Refer uninsured clients there or to the case manager to check current eligibility.
G.S. 90-21.5: a minor may consent to care for STIs and other reportable diseases, pregnancy (not sterilization or abortion), substance or alcohol abuse, and emotional disturbance.
Emancipated minors may consent. The age of majority is 18.
Insurance statements sent to a parent could reveal a teen’s confidential visit. Coordinate with billing or free public health clinics.
Suspected child abuse or neglect: report to county DSS (G.S. 7B-301). A disabled adult needing protection: report to county DSS (G.S. 108A-102).

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
bullets: Source: Module 47 study guide, pp. 2802–2804 (Outcome 47.7; Box 47.2; key terms).
Part B’s “20% co-payment” is technically 20% coinsurance, plus a premium and deductible.
People 65+ without 10 work years can usually buy Part A.
Medigap letters are federally standardized (different in Massachusetts, Minnesota, Wisconsin). Medigap works only with Original Medicare.
HRAs are employer-funded only. Employees may add to an HSA.
ACA: Medicaid expansion became optional for states after a 2012 Supreme Court ruling. The mandate penalty dropped to $0 in 2019.
The No Surprises Act (2022) protects most insured clients from surprise out-of-network emergency bills.
CHIP was created in 1997. COBRA and special enrollment were added for discharge planning.

mnemonics.name: “Happy People Pick Cheap Insurance”
mnemonics.text: Most to least restrictive: HMO → POS → PPO → CDHP → Indemnity.

mnemonics.name: MediCARE vs. MediCAID
mnemonics.text: CARE for the aged and disabled; AID for low income.

mnemonics.name: Medicare ABCD
mnemonics.text: A = Admitted (hospital, SNF, hospice, home health); B = Bills from providers, outpatient, DME, screenings; C = Combination (Advantage); D = Drugs.

pearls: Emergencies are covered under every plan. Never delay emergency care for a referral or network check.
HMO members usually need a PCP referral for a specialist. PPO members do not.
Medicare does not pay long-term custodial care. Medicaid is the main public payer for those who qualify.
If a client cannot afford a drug, ask the prescriber about generics and refer to social work.
redFlags: A client skips insulin, anticoagulants, or blood pressure pills because of cost. Assess, tell the prescriber, and arrange help before discharge.
A client with emergency symptoms wants to call the insurer first. Send them to emergency care now.
A pregnant client with high blood pressure and headache skipped care for cost. Assess and notify the provider first; enroll her in Medicaid after.

checks.q: A POS member wants an out-of-network surgeon a friend recommended. What should the nurse explain?
checks.a: POS allows it, but she will pay higher co-pays, coinsurance, and deductibles than for in-network care with a referral.

checks.q: A family earns slightly too much for Medicaid and cannot afford insurance for their 10-year-old. What should the nurse suggest?
checks.a: CHIP, through the local social services office (county DSS in NC) or the state program.

checks.q: A client met her $6,000 out-of-pocket maximum in March. She needs covered in-network surgery in June. What will she pay?
checks.a: The plan should pay 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the plan year. She still pays premiums and should confirm with her plan.

checks.q: A new graduate says, “Medicare Advantage is the same as Medigap.” How should the preceptor correct this?
checks.a: Advantage (Part C) replaces Original Medicare with a private bundled plan. Medigap supplements Original Medicare. They are not used together.

checks.q: An uninsured client with diabetes and a glucose of 312 is out of metformin but stable. After telling the provider, what next?
checks.a: Connect him with enrollment help and a social worker today. Medicare does not cover adults just for having diabetes.
